description: We are team ASTROS SPACE, a dedicated group of software developers, AI practitioners, and project managers passionate about building innovative, scientifically grounded solutions for space exploration and STEM education. Armed with strong technical expertise across Python, Dart/Flutter web development, workflow automation, and machine learning, our team excels at translating complex NASA data and real-world system mechanics into intuitive, user-friendly digital experiencesBy joining ASTROS SPACE
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer (Mars Base: Mission Control)
Developed by team ASTROS SPACE for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Cairo), the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based 3D educational game where players aged 7–15 act as rookie Mission Controllers managing a fictional Mars outpost. Built using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js, the platform challenges users to balance six vital life-support systems (Oxygen, Water, Food, Energy, Radiation Protection, and Temperature Control) across four progressive missions while handling realistic crises like dust storms and air leaks. The game emphasizes systems thinking through immediate visual feedback, a privacy-first local design requiring no accounts, and a Mission Brief system that links every decision to real NASA and Canadian Space Agency science.
details:
• What it does or how does it work: The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 3D educational management game where a young player acts as a rookie Mission Controller for a Martian science outpost. Across four progressive missions (13 total events), players walk an astronaut avatar around a 3D base using keyboard or touch controls, investigating highlighted systems and choosing responses to events like dust storms, air leaks, or radiation alerts. Every choice updates a six-resource engine (Oxygen, Water, Food, Energy, Radiation Protection, and Temperature Control) and is summarized in a Mission Brief with deltas, timelines, and NASA science cards.
  • What benefits does it have: It teaches children aged 7–15 complex systems thinking ("one decision affects many systems") through short, friendly decisions with no time pressure, no violence, and no punitive "game over" screens. If resources run out, a supportive "Stabilization Protocol" lets players retry. It also features AstroBot, a pre-mission assistant that answers space questions from a curated encyclopedia with source links, jargon definitions, and collectible badges.
  • What is the intended impact of the project: The project aims to make space STEM education accessible, engaging, and grounded in real engineering trade-offs. By connecting game decisions to actual NASA and Canadian Space Agency science, it inspires curiosity about space exploration and helps children understand the interconnected nature of life-support systems used in missions like Artemis.
  • What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project: The project frontend is built using React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 8, with global state managed via Zustand. The 3D world is rendered using Three.js through @react-three/fiber and @react-three/drei, built entirely from primitive geometry. Development tools included Git/GitHub, ESLint, and VS Code, with static production deployment hosted on Vercel. AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Google Antigravity, OpenAI Codex) were used to help draft code, documentation summaries, and knowledge bases, which were thoroughly reviewed by the human team.
  • How is your project creative: It creatively combines a fully walkable, browser-based 3D Mars base (built without external 3D assets) with a personal astronaut identity system, including an in-browser webcam/upload helmet portrait studio. Instead of traditional win/lose mechanics, it uses a constructive Mission Brief and a curiosity-driven AstroBot assistant that rewards players with space badges.
  • What factors did your team consider: The team prioritized child-friendly design features (large touch targets, short sentences, icons, and clear color/word resource states rather than color alone). They also emphasized strict privacy (no accounts, databases, or API keys required; local storage only)and scientific honesty—ensuring all game numbers are explicitly labeled as normalised educational indicators rather than physical measurements, while accurately paraphrasing real space agency facts.
